questions.q: Why does this lesson treat deployment documentation as part of the deliverable rather than paperwork added afterward?
options: Because a capability only the implementation team understands isn't actually deployable -- a checklist, a rollback plan, and a decision record are what make it real for everyone else
Because Meridian's board requires documentation purely as a formality with no real use
Because documentation replaces the need for Lesson 17's test plan
Because this course requires a written artifact for every lesson regardless of relevance
questions.explain: The checklist, rollback plan, and ADR are what let people outside the implementation team trust and operate what was built -- not a formality bolted on at the end.

questions.q: Why does St. Catherine's pilot go live first, per this lesson's reasoning?
options: Because it is the smallest and easiest hospital system to manage

Because its mature, structured process makes it the most likely to catch and precisely describe a real defect, turning the pilot into a genuine quality gate before the more trust-sensitive systems go live
Because Lesson 13 ranked it as having the fewest requirements
Because Technical Architecture's instance decision required it to go first
questions.explain: Piloting with the most capable, most mature process first means real defects get caught and clearly described, protecting Lakeshore's and Prairie View's later, more trust-sensitive go-lives.

questions.q: Why can the rollback plan be scoped to St. Catherine's domain alone, instead of the whole platform?
options: Because Lakeshore and Prairie View use a completely separate ServiceNow instance
Because Domain Separation keeps each hospital system's configuration and data genuinely distinct, so rolling back one domain's cutover doesn't touch domains that haven't gone live yet
Because a rollback plan is never actually domain-specific in any ServiceNow implementation
Because St. Catherine's legacy system was already decommissioned before go-live
questions.explain: Domain Separation's genuine structural isolation is exactly what makes a domain-scoped rollback possible -- Lakeshore and Prairie View are unaffected either way.

questions.q: What does the checklist's "legacy stays live through the pilot window" line actually guarantee, and why does it matter to Prairie View even though Prairie View isn't piloting first?
options: It guarantees nothing in practice and is only a courtesy statement

It confirms that no system's legacy process is switched off before its own replacement is confirmed working -- directly answering Prairie View's requirement, from Lesson 13, for proof this isn't a repeat of the forced consolidation
It means St. Catherine's will never actually go live on the new platform
It only applies to the integration layer, not to the help-desk process itself
questions.explain: Writing this into every system's own checklist -- St. Catherine's included -- is the honest, written proof behind Lesson 14's answer to Prairie View's trust concern, not a verbal promise.

questions.q: What four parts does this chapter's Architecture Decision Record use, following Technical Architecture's own ADR format?
options: Summary, Risks, Budget, Sign-off
Context, Options considered, Decision, Consequences
Problem, Solution, Timeline, Owner
Background, Stakeholders, Requirements, Approval
questions.explain: Context, Options, Decision, and Consequences are the exact four parts Technical Architecture's ADR lesson taught, applied here to the Prairie View integration-pattern decision.
